Deadline 11 days away, sales brochure only received now — insufficient time to consider

Ms. Au of Wang Tai House lives with her husband, three sons and a domestic helper. Her family is among the few households that have decided not to return the acquisition proposal letter before 8.31. Mrs. Au said she understands and knows that she will inevitably have to sell her property rights in the future, but feels that before 8.31 she is not physically or mentally prepared to make this decision.

As a mother of three, her family is her top priority — all three sons study in Tai Po, and she hopes as much as possible not to disrupt their lives, wanting to find a residence similar to Wang Fuk Court in the same district and rebuild a stable home. Yet she has yet to find an option that suits her family's needs — the sales brochure and detailed price list for the "Special Sales Scheme" were only released on 20 August, making it difficult for her to digest and consider the large amount of information in a short time; the Chung Nga Road West estate has inconvenient transport and will not be ready for occupation until 2030; buying a second-hand Home Ownership Scheme flat in Tai Po means she and her sons may not be able to bear the shadow of another major maintenance round; as for taking the money to the private market, she still has an outstanding mortgage that cannot be transferred, making it unaffordable and difficult to find a suitable home for a family of six.

All three options have their limitations, and Mrs. Au said helplessly, "They only gave me all the options to consider so late — I don't have enough time to think about this, I don't have the confidence to choose a suitable option for my family, I'm not physically or mentally ready to sign this letter of intent." "It's not about whether I want to or whether I would consider it — it's that I simply cannot decide… I can't rashly make such a major decision for my family."

Facing risks: worry and disappointment

Over the past few days, various parties have been reminding owners of the 8.31 deadline — the Wang Fuk Court property rights acquisition company previously sent a letter stating that failure to return the letter of intent before the deadline would be regarded as giving up participation in the long-term housing arrangement scheme; Financial Secretary Deputy Cheung Wai-lun also spoke up, saying the deadline is a "serious timeline" that will not be extended, and that legislation to resume ownership would be considered, with the outcome expected to be "substantially inferior" to the government's acquisition price.

Afraid of breaking down under mental pressure

Mrs. Au understands that the government needs to set a deadline to proceed, but as a disaster victim, she notes the government often says "putting people's feelings first," yet at the same time states "once we've decided on something, there's no going back" — a position that is both heartbreaking and disappointing. She does not shy away from saying she is worried about the risks she will have to bear and indeed feels enormous pressure, but at this stage "I really cannot force myself to make this decision," "I'm very afraid of making the wrong decision, and I'm also very afraid that I won't be able to cope with the mental pressure and will break down."

Mrs. Au had also considered returning the letter of intent first, but she said that after the 6.30 deadline passed, some neighbours reported that only upon signing did they learn the terms included giving up items inside the flat and not being allowed to photocopy the sales and purchase agreement, causing her to worry about facing unacceptable terms.

Mrs. Au reiterated that once the government announced the acquisition, she and her husband had been monitoring the prices of Tai Po estates and had enquired with the explanation team about matters such as estate insurance and maintenance, but had never received a reply; with the government and Hip Hing releasing different information in a "toothpaste-squeezing" manner as the deadline approached, "As an owner, I am not physically or mentally ready to make such a major decision in such a short time."

Hoping the government will extend the deadline and wait for the investigation report before selling the flat

Although the government has made clear it will not extend the deadline, Mrs. Au still hopes the government can stand in the disaster victims' shoes and understand that this matter is "a lifelong shadow," truly putting "people's feelings first" by giving flexibility and room according to the different needs of residents, extending the deadline so they have enough time to carefully consider and make important, long-term decisions they will not regret for their families.

She has also always believed that, in principle, the sale of property rights should wait until the investigation report is released and the cause of the fire and responsibility clarified; she also finds it hard to accept using charitable funds to acquire property rights. However, the independent committee has already been granted an extension and is expected to complete its report only at the end of October.

"As a resident, what I really can't let go of is that I want there to be a proper sequence — let me understand why this happened at Wang Fuk, why we encountered this misfortune, and then tell me what choices I have, that I have to move forward, that I can't go back to Wang Fuk. I think with that sequence, as a resident, I would feel more comfortable and more accepting about selling a place I love so much."

"Not being able to wait for the independent investigation report before selling the flat is, for me, a regret."

Even if reluctant, a new home must be built

The government recently announced that 94.7% of owners have returned the letter, with only about a hundred households remaining. Mrs. Au said the numbers are meaningless to her, since whether to sell property rights is a decision based on family needs, "it's not a game of majority rule." She also frankly said she cannot predict what will happen after 8.31: "If they really insist on acting according to legal principles rather than what they call putting feelings first, there's nothing I can do — I'll be forced to accept it and see how things develop next."

Regarding Cheung Wai-lun's remark that some owners have not returned the letter because they are dissatisfied with the acquisition price, Mrs. Au said this is not her thinking, and stressed she is not trying to confront the government. She has always believed that the most responsible decision for her family is to see the road ahead clearly before deciding. If a suitable option is found, "actually I am very willing to sign this letter of intent."

Having often mentioned in past interviews how much she loves the Wang Fuk Court place and the bonds with her neighbours, Mrs. Au frankly said she knows full well things cannot be reversed, and selling the property rights is the only option, "whether I like it or not, it's my only choice." Letting go of Wang Fuk and moving away from Wang Fuk is an inevitable fact and a decision forced by circumstances: "Even if I can't bear to part with it, I have to take a step forward and rebuild a new home… some things you really have to move forward on, some things you have to accept."

"Where the people are, home is" — these are words she has often said to her three sons since the disaster. "I hope that even if neighbours can't bear to part with Wang Fuk, they will let go of Wang Fuk and move forward to start new lives of their own."
